title: TANESCO management contract with NETGroup
point: Dar es Salaam, seat of the state power utility TANESCO (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Made power-sector reform a lending condition in 1993. The contract was paid through a World Bank trust fund (money from Sweden's Sida), and the Bank had to approve each stage (Ghanadan and Eberhard 2007).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Tanzania's August 2001 letter of intent to the IMF said the government had decided to hire a management company to run TANESCO from November 2001, and to let TANESCO raise average tariffs. The July 2003 letter listed TANESCO among utilities still to be privatized.

conditions: IMF letter of intent, 31 August 2001: engage a management company for TANESCO and raise the average electricity tariff. IMF letter of intent, 10 July 2003: medium-term focus on privatizing large utilities including TANESCO. World Bank: sector reform a lending condition since 1993 (Ghanadan and Eberhard).

companies.name: NETGroup Solutions
companies.role: Managed TANESCO from May 2002 to December 2006; paid about US$18–19 million, mostly tied to revenue collection
companies.hq: South Africa (city not given in sources)

community: In 2003 more than 1,280 workers (about 21% of staff) were retrenched; staff fell from 6,540 (2002) to 4,787 (2005). Residential tariffs rose about 39% from 2001 to 2006 while large industrial tariffs fell 22–28%. Bills for homes using over 50 kWh a month nearly tripled from 2000 to 2005 while prices overall rose about 25%. The low-use 'lifeline' block was cut from 100 to 50 kWh. About 15,000–20,000 customers were cut off each month; from May 2002 to June 2005 there were 713,720 disconnections against 569,770 customers. Load shedding reached 12–16 hours a day in 2006. All figures: Ghanadan and Eberhard (2007).
suppression: The government refused a parliamentary request to make the contract public (SADOCC news, 2002).
outcome: Revenue collection nearly doubled, but losses and reliability did not improve and new connections fell short of targets (Ghanadan and Eberhard). The contract ended in December 2006; TANESCO was not sold.

title: Argentine railway privatisation
point: Once station, Buenos Aires, hub of the national rail network (approximate stand-in for a country-wide case)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Signed a 1990 restructuring program with the state railway (FA) and the ministry, the first official document to propose taking FA out of passenger service (Wikipedia). IPS reports the Bank recommended privatization and lent US$800 million to pay severance to 80,000 public workers who lost their jobs.

conditions: 1990 FA–Ministry–World Bank restructuring program: private concessionaires only on freight lines; intercity passenger services (except Buenos Aires–Mar del Plata) to end on 1 January 1993 unless provinces took them over. World Bank severance loan of US$800 million (IPS).

companies.name: Trenes de Buenos Aires (TBA)
companies.role: Commuter concession on the Mitre and Sarmiento lines; revoked May 2012

companies.name: Metropolitano
companies.role: Commuter concessions; San Martín line revoked 2004, two more in 2007

community: Rail jobs fell from 95,000 to 15,000; closures of rail-supply firms cost another 20,000 jobs (IPS, citing engineer Elido Veschi). The network shrank from 35,000 km to 8,500 km. Several interior cities lost their train to the capital and some villages became ghost towns. By 2002 subsidies to concessionaires cost about US$400 million a year, roughly what the state had spent running the network. A 2003 regulator report found 70% of inspected cars had faults such as brakes. By late 2003, 389 commuter passengers had died in accidents (IPS).
killed_note: IPS counts 389 commuter deaths in accidents by late 2003, and the 2012 Once crash killed 51 (BBC via Wikipedia), but no source cited here ties a specific death toll to the World Bank-backed program, so no figure is entered.
outcome: On 22 February 2012 a TBA train crashed at Once station, killing 51 and injuring over 700; TBA's concession was revoked in May 2012. In 2015 Congress passed a law returning the railways to the state (Nuevos Ferrocarriles Argentinos).

sources.title: Railway privatisation in Argentina

confidence_note: The World Bank's restructuring document cited by Wikipedia could not be opened; the Bank's role rests on Wikipedia and IPS. The privatisation law (Law 23,696, 1989) was Argentina's own.

title: Luanshya mines sale to Binani (RAMCOZ)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Fraser and Lungu (2007) list repeated Bank loan conditions to privatize the state copper firm ZCCM: PIRC II (1993), ERIP (1995), ESAC II (1996) and a 1999 credit.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: ESAF loans (1995, 1999) also required ZCCM privatization plans; HIPC debt relief depended on IMF and Bank reviews (Fraser and Lungu).

conditions: World Bank PIRC II (1993): study options to privatize ZCCM; ERIP and IMF ESAF (1995), ESAC II (1996), and 1999 Bank and IMF loans: carry out ZCCM privatization (Fraser and Lungu 2007, For Whom the Windfalls?).

companies.name: Binani Group
companies.role: Bought 85% of Roan Antelope Mining Corporation of Zambia (RAMCOZ: Luanshya and Baluba mines) in 1997

community: Binani soon abandoned the investment. By November 2000 the state bank ZANACO moved to put RAMCOZ in receivership, 5,000 jobs were at risk, and the power company cut supply over nearly US$10 million in unpaid bills (IRIN). Miners held a sit-in to demand money owed. The mines then sat idle for three years (Fraser and Lungu). Across ZCCM, jobs fell from about 31,000 at sale to 19,145 in 2001.
suppression: Paramilitary police were sent to the plant to head off demonstrations when the receivership was announced (IRIN, November 2000).
outcome: In 2004 a Swiss investor (J&W, a subsidiary of Enya) bought the assets, now Luanshya Mines Plc (Fraser and Lungu).

title: Gécamines voluntary departure program
point: Likasi, where the ex-workers who complained to the Inspection Panel live (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The Private Sector Development and Competitiveness credit (US$120 million, 2003) and a US$25 million tranche of the Economic Recovery Credit paid for severance of 10,655 Gécamines workers (World Bank management response). Ex-workers told the Inspection Panel the Bank made its funding depend on large staff cuts.

conditions: PSDC Project (IDA Credit 3815-DRC), Component 2, parastatal reform: finance severance to shrink Gécamines' workforce (about 11,200 eligible). The project document calls the cuts government policy.

companies.name: Gécamines
companies.role: State mining company that cut its workforce

community: 10,655 workers left between August 2003 and February 2004, with average pay-outs of US$4,083 (Bank figures). The ex-workers say wage arrears, final settlements, housing and other benefits went unpaid, and that they were forced into poverty. A 2006 evaluation found most started some income activity, but only about 100 small firms were launched and 230 of 1,200 hectares set aside were farmed.
suppression: Ex-workers' letters to the Bank in early 2009 went unanswered; Bank management admitted it 'did not respond to all the emails'.
outcome: In August 2011 the Inspection Panel chose not to investigate after management promised an action plan (school fees, health care, pension access, about US$12–14 million re-allocated). The Panel said the Bank's handling of risks 'could have been better'.

title: Egypt 2024 bread and fuel price rises
point: Cairo (approximate; subsidised bread is sold nationwide)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Expanded Egypt's loan programme to $8 billion in March 2024. Conditions reported include a currency float, subsidy cuts on food, fuel and services, and ending fuel subsidies by December 2025 (The National).

conditions: The National reports the IMF plan to bring fuel prices to market levels by end-2025, with the government free to set the pace. Mada Masr reports subsidy cuts are part of policy recommendations tied to the $8 billion loan. The subsidised loaf rose from 5 to 20 piastres in June 2024, first rise since 1989 (IFPRI).
community: About 70 million people rely on subsidised bread daily (Mada Masr); IFPRI counted 73 million beneficiaries in 2023. Fuel prices rose three times in 2024, with diesel up 17.3% in October (Peoples Dispatch; The National). Electricity rose by up to 50% in September 2024 (The National). The supply ministry says 850,000 people were removed from the subsidy system after June 2026 (AFP via Kuwait Times).
outcome: Prime Minister Madbouly said the government would review IMF targets and timelines 'if people cannot bear it' (The National, October 2024). Further removals from ration lists were planned for 2027 (Kuwait Times).

title: Ghana 2015 hiring freeze and unposted nurses
point: Accra, seat of the ministries of health and finance (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a three-year, $918 million Extended Credit Facility on 3 April 2015, relying on wage restraint, payroll clean-up and 'limited net hiring' (IMF Press Release 15/159).

conditions: The IMF's first review in August 2015 described a 'net hiring freeze' with exemptions for health and education (IMF Press Release 15/393). 3News reported the IMF wanted the wage bill cut to about 35% of tax revenue, from about 50% in 2014.
community: Over 2,000 trained nurses and midwives who finished national service were left waiting for posts; the Finance Ministry said there was no money (3News, July 2015). A 2021 ActionAid report says the hiring freeze and cap on wage rises limited hiring of teachers, nurses and doctors (Daily Graphic).
outcome: The Coalition of Unemployed Nurses and Midwives threatened demonstrations; the health minister asked for time without a deadline (3News). ActionAid in 2021 called for an end to wage bill constraints (Daily Graphic).

title: Guinea 2006 fuel price strikes and killings
point: Conakry (approximate); killings were also reported in Labé

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Ran a Staff-Monitored Program from 2005. In January 2006 its directors advised that petroleum prices move in line with world prices (IMF PIN 06/07).

conditions: The May 2005 letter of intent fixed the 2005 wage bill at 2.9% of GDP and recorded the 1 March 2005 move to a market exchange rate (IMF). IMF directors advised letting fuel prices follow world prices (IMF, 2006). IRIN reports the May 2006 fuel price rises were made in line with IMF policy to end fuel subsidies.
community: The Guinean franc lost 38% of its value after March 2005; inflation reached about 28–30% (IRIN). A graduate civil servant's monthly pay fell 40% in value to about US$40, while a 50-kg sack of rice cost over US$25 (IRIN, June 2006).
suppression: During the June 2006 strike, security forces shot protesters, many of them students denied exams. HRW gathered accounts of 13 killings in Conakry and Labé, two rapes, and beatings in police custody with release only on bribes. Earlier, in March 2006, the president's guards fired on youths, killing a bystander (IRIN).
killed_note: Official toll 11; local civil society groups counted 21 killed by security force gunfire (Human Rights Watch). Mail & Guardian reported at least 18 dead and 83 wounded from witnesses and hospitals.
outcome: The March 2006 strike won a promise of 30% civil service pay rises and a minimum wage (IRIN). Unions kept demanding lower fuel and rice prices; larger strikes followed in January 2007.

title: Greece May 2010 General Strike and Marfin Bank Deaths
point: Marfin Egnatia bank branch on Stadiou Avenue, central Athens (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a three-year Stand-By Arrangement of about €30 billion in May 2010, part of €110 billion with euro-area loans (IMF press release 10/176).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB (with the IMF, the 'troika')
lenders.role: Euro-area countries lent €80 billion on the same program terms (IMF press release 10/176).

conditions: IMF press release 10/176 (May 2010): measures for 2010 'involve a reduction of public sector wages and pension outlays', part of spending cuts and tax rises worth 11% of GDP, aiming for a deficit under 3% of GDP by 2014. WBUR/AP: the bill cut civil servants' pay and pensions and raised consumer taxes, to save about €30 billion through 2012, as conditions set by the IMF and European countries.
community: On 5 May 2010, during a 48-hour general strike against the package, attackers threw petrol bombs into the Marfin bank branch. Three bank employees died from smoke: Angeliki Papathanasopoulou (32, reportedly four months pregnant), Epaminondas Tsakalis (36) and Paraskevi Zoulia (35) (To Vima). Organisers said about 350,000 people joined the strike nationwide (EUobserver); about 20,000 marched in Thessaloniki (WBUR/AP).
suppression: About eight protesters were beaten by police near parliament and taken to hospital, two reportedly in serious condition, according to the Athens municipal workers' union (EUobserver).
killed_note: Three Marfin bank employees, per the fire brigade and police (EUobserver) and To Vima. They were killed by petrol bombs thrown by unknown attackers, not by police.
outcome: Parliament passed the package. Greece's Supreme Court later set aside the acquittal of several bank executives over missing fire safety equipment (To Vima). In July 2026 police arrested two people and sought a third over the firebombing (Reuters).

title: Greece Memorandum Pension Cuts
point: Syntagma Square, where pensioner Dimitris Christoulas died in April 2012

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: With the European Commission and ECB, set up the loan mechanism; the Greek government told the Council of Europe that meeting the Memoranda timetable was a prerequisite for each loan payment.

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: Co-authors of the Memoranda annexed to Acts 3845/2010 and 4046/2012 (Greek government observations to the ECSR).

conditions: The Greek government stated that loan terms were tied to fiscal measures in the Memoranda (Acts 3845/2010 and 4046/2012). Pension laws it listed: a 3–14% 'solidarity' deduction from pensions above €1,400 a month (from August 2010); a further 6–10% for under-60s above €1,700 (August 2011); a 40% cut on the part above €1,000 for under-55s and 20% above €1,200 for over-55s (November 2011); a 12% cut on the part above €1,300 (January 2012). Holiday bonuses were reduced to fixed sums (Greek government observations, 2012).
community: Pensioners lost part of their monthly pensions under each law. On 4 April 2012 Dimitris Christoulas, a 77-year-old retired pharmacist, shot himself in Syntagma Square; his note blamed the government for cutting his pension so far that he could no longer live on it. Time tied his death to cuts demanded by the EU and IMF as bailout conditions.
suppression: After Christoulas's death, hundreds gathered at the site; youths threw petrol bombs and riot police used tear gas (Time).
killed_note: Not counted as a killing. Time reports one suicide (Dimitris Christoulas) linked by his note to pension cuts.
outcome: In December 2012 the European Committee of Social Rights found that the 2010–2011 pension cuts violated Article 12§3 of the European Social Charter (complaint 76/2012, IKA-ETAM v. Greece). The Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers adopted Resolution ResChS(2014)7 in July 2014.

title: Portugal Troika Programme: Health Fees, Pension Cuts and Mass Protests
point: Lisbon, site of the 2011–2012 strikes and marches (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Co-lender in Portugal's €78 billion bailout of May 2011 (Mail & Guardian/AP); co-signer of the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (Eurofound).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The other troika members; the European Commission published the Memorandum of Understanding.

conditions: The May 2011 Memorandum of Understanding required Portugal to 'Reduce pensions above EUR 1,500', freeze most pensions in 2012, freeze public wages in 2012 and 2013, cut public staff by 1–2% a year, 'review and increase overall NHS moderating fees', cap unemployment benefit at 18 months, and raise VAT on electricity and gas from 6%. It also called for a 'fiscal devaluation' — a large cut in employers' social contributions (European Commission MoU; Eurofound).
community: Health co-payments rose from 2011 to 2013: primary care €2.25 to €5.00, emergency visits €9.40 to €20.60. The odds of reporting unmet medical need more than doubled between 2010 and 2012; in a 2013 survey in two deprived Lisbon-area towns, 45.1% could not afford medicines (Legido-Quigley et al., Health Policy 2016). A general strike on 24 November 2011 stopped flights, trains and factories (AP). On 15 September 2012 an estimated 500,000 people marched in Lisbon against a plan to raise workers' social contributions from 11% to 18% while cutting employers' (Eurofound).
outcome: The government dropped the contribution plan after the September 2012 protests (Eurofound). Health fee levels stayed in place through 2015, after the bailout ended (Health Policy 2016).

title: Bosnia 2010 War Veterans' Benefit Cuts and Sarajevo Clashes

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Bosnia's €1.2 billion ($1.62–1.74 billion) Stand-By Arrangement required both entities to cut wages and budget payments (RFE/RL; Al Jazeera).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Tied a $100 million structural reform loan to a review of payments to war-related beneficiaries (RFE/RL/Reuters).

conditions: Under the IMF deal, the Federation and Republika Srpska agreed to cut public wages and payments to budget beneficiaries by 10%. War-related benefits made up about 40% of the Federation budget (RFE/RL/Reuters, 2009). Al Jazeera (2010): the cuts were required to meet the conditions of the IMF loan; parliament passed stricter eligibility rules, with a property census as the main test from January 2011.

title: Thailand 1997 Finance Company Closures and VAT Rise

title: Zambia 1995 mining laws and development agreements
point: Kitwe, centre of the Copperbelt mining towns (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Reform of the Investment Act was a condition of the Bank's 1993 PIRC II loan; the 1995 Investment Act and Mines and Minerals Act followed (Fraser and Lungu, for Christian Aid).

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Later Fund and Bank loans (ESAF, ESAC II and others) required the state mining firm ZCCM to be broken up and sold; HIPC debt relief from 1996 added leverage (Fraser and Lungu).

conditions: Change the investment law as a condition of the World Bank's 1993 PIRC II loan, then unbundle and privatise ZCCM under later IMF and World Bank loans (Fraser and Lungu). The 1995 Mines and Minerals Act let the state sign secret 'development agreements' with each buyer.
community: Royalties: the Act set 3% of net back value, but most buyers negotiated 0.6% of gross revenue. Mining tax was 25% against 35% for manufacturing, terms were frozen for 15 to 20 years, and firms were not liable for pollution above ZCCM's past discharge levels during those years. Mine jobs fell from about 31,000 when the first mine was sold in 1997 to 19,145 in 2001; the Chamber of Mines counted 19,900 direct jobs in 2004. About 45% of mine workers had no permanent contract by 2006, and contract workers were paid about half of Mopani's wage for the same work. Mine hospitals and anti-malaria spraying were cut; by 2004 about a quarter of recorded Copperbelt deaths were from malaria (all from Fraser and Lungu).
suppression: Unions told Fraser and Lungu that firms dismissed members of shadow union committees, and contract workers were kept out of union representation.
outcome: The agreements were kept from MPs, unions and regulators. Pambazuka reports exemptions covered customs duty to pollution penalties.

sources.title: For Whom the Windfalls? Winners and Losers in the Privatisation of Zambia's Copper Mines

title: Portugal troika labour law changes
point: Lisbon, seat of the government that signed the 2011 program (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The September 2011 letter of intent and Memorandum of Understanding set cuts in severance pay and unemployment benefits.

lenders.name: European Commission and European Central Bank
lenders.role: Co-lenders; the ETUC says the troika insisted on stricter rules for extending collective agreements.

conditions: IMF letter of intent, September 1, 2011: severance for new open-ended contracts 'reduced from 30 to 10 days per year of tenure', capped at 12 months, with the 3-month minimum dropped (the memorandum of economic policies in the same package gives 20 days); maximum unemployment benefit cut to 18 months and capped at 2.5 times the social support index. The May 2011 memorandum also changed rules for extending collective agreements (Addison et al.).
community: From October 2012 sector agreements could be extended to a whole industry only if signatory employers had more than half its workers. Workers covered by newly published agreements fell from 1,894,846 in 2008 to 327,662 in 2012 and 242,676 in 2013, an 87% drop (Addison, Portugal and Vilares, from ministry data). Extended agreements fell from 116 in 2010 to nine in 2013 (ETUC). In seven of ten manufacturing firms studied, managers cut overtime pay on their own (Távora and González).
outcome: In June 2014 the extension rule was loosened for sectors dominated by small firms. Addison et al. argue total coverage under all existing agreements barely moved (90.5% in 2008, 89.2% in 2013) because old agreements stayed in force.
